messages:
ravi: Quick question about the new fennel-6b we pulled in for eval — license text has a clause that reads something like 'no commercial redistribution or hosting without explicit permission'. Can we expose this model via Redwood Hosted API, or would that be considered redistribution/hosting? Also: are we allowed to ship quantized checkpoints to Dedicated customers? @sara :thinking:

sara: Short answer: it depends on the exact license language. Some model licenses forbid 'providing the model as a hosted service' (i.e., offering inference via a 3rd-party API) and others only restrict binary redistribution. Need to see the exact clause. Generally: Hosted API is risky if the license explicitly bans 'offering as a service' or 'hosting for third-party access'.

ana: From infra standpoint — if we only serve from our infra (no customer gets the weights), that's usually fine unless the license says 'no offering hosted inference'. For Dedicated we do ship artifacts into customer-managed instances; that is definitely redistribution in most license defs.

mike: On the attribution side — the license also mentions retaining NOTICE and attribution in downstream products. Do we need to surface that in the Console or in customer docs (terms)? :memo:

sara: Yes, include the NOTICE/attribution in product metadata and in the Dedicated/private onboarding docs. For Hosted, we should include the model's attribution in the model metadata page and in any marketing that highlights the model. You do NOT usually need to add attribution into every model response payload, unless the license expressly requires in-band attribution.

ravi: Thanks. There's also a 'derivative weights' line that might block quantization/optimization:

```
Section 4(b): "No creation or distribution of derivative model weights or converted binaries (including quantized, pruned or otherwise transformed checkpoints) without express written permission from the original authors."
```

If that's present, does converting to 4-bit count as a derivative?

sara: Most counsels consider any transformation that results in a new binary (quantized checkpoint) a derivative. So converting and then distributing is risky. Converting for internal inference (i.e., we keep the converted file on our servers and never hand it out) may be less risky but still borderline depending on jurisdiction and exact phrasing. We should assume "derivative" includes quantized checkpoints unless we get a waiver.

ana: Operationally, that means: Hosted -> host quantized artifacts internally only if legal approves. Dedicated -> avoid shipping converted weights; instead ship original upstream artifact and provide conversion scripts that run on customer side (or have them run the conversion themselves). Private -> fine to let customer run conversion in their environment, we can provide the tooling.

mike: Could we offer a paid addendum that allows customers to receive optimized/quantized binaries? i.e., negotiate redistribution rights into enterprise contracts?

sara: Yes. We can negotiate a redistribution addendum or licensing fee that grants rights to distribute derived binaries. I'll coordinate with partnerships to draft a template addendum.

ravi: Great. Action items for clarity: 1) legal draft internal guidance for fennel-6b and similar licenses; 2) product add gating/notice in onboarding for models with restrictive clauses; 3) eng infra ensure no converted artifacts are stored in shared buckets unless approved.

sara: I'll draft the guidance and checklist (incl. sample contractual language). ETA: EOD tomorrow. cc @ana @mike :white_check_mark:
